content: Here is the reformulated content: Study Summaries and Methodologies Retnakumari 2012 Study Design: This was a cross-sectional descriptive study. Participants: The study was conducted among children attending the immunization clinic at Sree Avittam Thirunal Hospital, Medical College, Trivandrum, as well as children attending randomly selected Anganwadis and daycare centers in Trivandrum, Kerala. The study included children aged 12–36 months and their mothers, who were both examined and interviewed. Risk of Bias: The risk of bias was judged as unclear across multiple domains, including selection bias (random sequence generation and allocation concealment), performance bias (blinding of participants and personnel), detection bias (blinding of outcome assessment), reporting bias (selective reporting), and other potential biases. Robinson 2009 Study Design: This was a prospective cohort study. Participants: Between 1998 and 2002, all non-pregnant women aged 20–34 years in Southampton, UK, who were registered with a general practitioner, were invited to participate in the Southampton Women’s Survey (SWS). Women who became pregnant during the study were followed throughout their pregnancy, and their children were monitored during infancy and early childhood. Interventions: Infants were visited within two weeks of their six-month and twelve-month birthdays. Milk feeding history over the preceding six months was recorded during these visits. Breastfeeding duration was defined based on the date of the last breastfeeding session. Risk of Bias: The risk of bias was unclear in areas such as confounding, participant selection, classification of exposures, departures from intended exposures, incomplete outcome data, measurement of outcomes, and selective reporting. Schwarz 2009 Study Design: This study combined cohort and cross-sectional methodologies. Participants: Postmenopausal women aged 50–79 years were enrolled at one of 40 Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) clinical centers across the United States. Participants were included in either a clinical trial (CT) involving approximately 64,500 women or an observational study (OS) involving about 100,000 women. Eligibility required the ability to provide informed consent and an expectation of residing in the study area for at least three years post-enrollment. Women with medical conditions predicting survival of less than three years or conditions inconsistent with study adherence (e.g., alcoholism, drug dependency, mental illness) were excluded. Interventions: At baseline, participants completed questionnaires on medical, reproductive, and family history, medication use, and lifestyle. Annual medical update forms were used to report hospitalizations and other outcomes. Breastfeeding history was recorded as a categorical variable based on cumulative lifetime duration. Outcomes: Cardiovascular disease and other outcomes were assessed prospectively. Hospitalizations and deaths due to coronary disease were confirmed through medical record reviews and adjudicated using death certificates and event descriptions. Risk of Bias: The risk of bias was unclear across multiple domains, including confounding, participant selection, classification of exposures, and reporting. Shrutha 2013 Study Design: This was a cross-sectional study. Participants: The study included children aged 3–5 years from a random sample of preschools in the Kanpur district, India. A two-stage cluster sampling technique was used. The district was divided into four geographical regions, and schools were randomly selected from each region to ensure equal representation. Eligible children were stratified by gender and randomly selected in proportion to the total number of students enrolled in each school, resulting in a sample size of approximately 2,000. Interventions: Data were collected using a pretested questionnaire in Hindi, which included questions on personal data, maternal feeding practices, and oral hygiene practices. Mothers were asked to select one of 35 alternatives for each question. Risk of Bias: The risk of bias was unclear in areas such as confounding, participant selection, classification of exposures, and reporting. Sichieri 2003 Study Design: This was a prospective cohort study. Participants: The Nurses’ Health Study II was established in 1989 with 116,671 female registered nurses who completed a mailed questionnaire about their parity, medical history, and lifestyle. For this study, the sample was restricted to women aged 24–40 years in 1989 who were not pregnant at baseline, had no more than one full-term pregnancy, and gave birth to one child in 1990 or 1991. Women with insulin use, hypoglycemic drug use, or thyroid disease were excluded. Interventions: Breastfeeding data were collected retrospectively in 1997. Women were asked to recall their lifetime breastfeeding history, including the duration of breastfeeding for each child and the timing of formula introduction. Outcomes: Weight change was assessed, and breastfeeding duration was categorized into exclusive breastfeeding periods of 0, 1–3, 4–7, 8–11, and 12 months or more. Risk of Bias: The risk of bias was unclear across multiple domains, including confounding, participant selection, classification of exposures, and reporting. Song 2020 Study Design: This was a cross-sectional study. Participants: Data were derived from a cross-sectional survey conducted as part of UNICEF-China’s Integrated Maternal and Child Health and Development (IMCHD) Project. A three-stage sampling procedure was used. First, 15 administrative villages in each selected county were chosen using probability proportional to size (PPS) sampling. Second, two natural villages were randomly selected from each administrative village using PPS. Third, eight households with children under five years old were randomly selected from each natural village, resulting in a total of 4,488 children surveyed. Interventions: Indicators for breastfeeding assessment (e.g., ever breastfed, duration of breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding, predominant breastfeeding, continued breastfeeding until 1 and 2 years) were extracted for all children. Outcomes: Obesity in children under five years of age was assessed. Overweight and obesity were defined as weight-for-height z-scores greater than 2 and 3 standard deviations above the WHO Child Growth Standards median, respectively. Risk of Bias: The risk of bias was unclear across multiple domains, including confounding, participant selection, classification of exposures, and reporting. Sowole 2006 Study Design: This was a cross-sectional study. Participants: The study included children aged 6 months to 5 years presenting at pediatric outpatient clinics in two urban areas (Ikeja and Surulere) and one rural area (Badagry) in Nigeria. Participants were randomly selected from these locations. Risk of Bias: The risk of bias was unclear across multiple domains, including confounding, participant selection, classification of exposures, and reporting. Stendel-Hollis 2013 Study Design: The Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) is a large, randomized, controlled study consisting of both a clinical trial (CT) and an observational study (OS) involving over 168,000 postmenopausal women. Participants: Eligibility required women to be postmenopausal, aged 50–79 years, free of conditions inconsistent with study adherence, and with an estimated survival of at least three years. Women unwilling to be randomized or ineligible for the clinical components were offered enrollment in the OS component. Women with prior breast cancer were excluded from the CT. Interventions: At baseline, participants completed questionnaires on medical, reproductive, and family history, medication use, and lifestyle. Annual updates were used to track hospitalizations and other outcomes. Outcomes: Outcomes included a wide range of health conditions, with confirmation of hospitalizations and deaths based on medical record reviews and adjudication using death certificates. Risk of Bias: The risk of bias was unclear across multiple domains, including confounding, participant selection, classification of exposures, and reporting.
